sources.title: Retama sphaerocarpa — WEB_BIOCON
sources.excerpt: Broom-form shrub; yellow axillary flowers; retama scrub and occasional rambla pioneers. The ecology section discusses Rhizobium and arbuscular mycorrhizal symbioses.

sources.title: Macrochloa tenacissima — WEB_BIOCON
sources.excerpt: Macrochloa tenacissima is also called Stipa tenacissima. A tussock grass of dry espartales; leaves roll and unroll with water conditions.

sources.title: Thymus hyemalis subsp. hyemalis — WEB_BIOCON
sources.excerpt: Aromatic low shrub with narrow rolled-margin leaves. Southeastern Iberian thyme scrub on varied substrates; the source distinguishes genus-level mycorrhizal evidence from species-specific evidence.

sources.title: Ephedra fragilis subsp. fragilis — WEB_BIOCON
sources.excerpt: Dioecious shrub with articulated green shoots and reduced leaves. Arid scrub on varied substrates, often calcareous or gypsum; gymnosperm cones are not flowers or ordinary fruits.

sources.title: Lycium intricatum — Herbari Virtual
sources.excerpt: Thorny shrub with tortuous branches, fleshy leaves and violet tubular flowers, associated with warm rocky coastal sites.

sources.title: Nerium oleander — Herbari Virtual
sources.excerpt: Evergreen shrub with leathery narrow leaves and terminal flower clusters. Recorded in non-saline wet places including ramblas. The source explicitly notes toxicity if ingested.

retama.description: Broom-form shrub with slender green shoots and yellow axillary flower clusters. The UAL account places it in retama scrub, sometimes pioneering ramblas, across varied substrates.

esparto.description: Robust tussock grass with long leaves that can roll into tubes. It forms dry grasslands known as espartales or atochares; this species identity is distinct from the habitat topic.

thyme.description: Low aromatic woody thyme with narrow rolled-margin leaves and pink flowers. The cited account concerns subsp. hyemalis in southeastern Iberian scrub and thyme communities.
thyme.name_note: Topic retains Thymus hyemalis; the principal detailed account is specifically subsp. hyemalis.

rosemary.description: Evergreen upright aromatic shrub with opposite narrow leaves, recurved margins and pale felted undersides. UAM records Rosmarinus officinalis and Salvia rosmarinus as synonyms.

ephedra_fragilis.description: Much-branched shrub with articulated green shoots and tiny reduced leaves. Male and female plants are separate; the illustration depicts a female form. The UAL account concerns subsp. fragilis.

ziziphus.description: Strongly thorny deciduous shrub forming dense rounded masses, with zigzag branches and three-veined leaves. Distinct from cultivated Ziziphus jujuba.

lycium.description: Thorny shrub with twisted branches, fleshy grey-green leaves and violet tubular flowers. The university account associates it with warm rocky coastal sites.

salsola.description: Shrub of semi-arid scrub recorded in the UAL flora table for Almería and the Alpujarras. Kew accepts Salsola webbii and records southern Spain and Morocco as its native range.
salsola.name_note: Retain Salsola webbii. Kew qualifies Salsola ericoides as not validly published and Anabasis tamariscifolia as sensu auct.; these aliases do not establish unrestricted name equivalence.

oleander.description: Evergreen shrub with narrow leathery leaves and terminal pink flower clusters. Occurs in non-saline wet places including ramblas; toxic if ingested.

tamarix.description: Genus-level tamarisk topic. The university habitat account records several Tamarix species with oleander in warm Mediterranean watercourse vegetation; the pictured taxon is not identified to species.
tamarix.name_note: Tamarix spp. intentionally remains genus-level. A T. gallica botanical illustration reference is an example, not an identification.

findings.label: Source-specific watercourse and jujube communities
findings.text: UAL describes warm Mediterranean watercourses with oleander and several Tamarix species. At Torre García, Ziziphus lotus dominates jujube scrub; Lycium intricatum is a companion and Thymus hyemalis occurs in openings. Its Tabernas discussion also names rosemary scrub. These are habitat descriptions, not mixed-planting trials.

findings.label: Retama ecology and symbiosis context
findings.text: The UAL Retama account describes photosynthetic green shoots, short-lived leaves, Rhizobium symbiosis and arbuscular mycorrhiza. It places the plant in retama scrub and sometimes as a rambla pioneer, from sea level to 1500 m. These species-specific observations do not imply that every legume fixes nitrogen or establish a treatment recommendation.

findings.label: Esparto leaves respond to water conditions
findings.text: The UAL account describes rolled leaves that reduce water loss and can unfold in wetter conditions, arbuscular mycorrhiza, and regrowth from underground parts after fire. It describes dry tussock grasslands from sea level to 1500 m in southeastern Iberia; this is not a planting-success prediction.

findings.label: Winter thyme avoids summer drought through seasonal timing
findings.text: The cited subsp. hyemalis account describes reproduction before summer drought, subsequent summer rest and rolled hairy leaf margins. It explicitly lacks species-specific mycorrhizal evidence, although other Thymus species have been studied. No inoculation recommendation is established.

findings.label: Ephedra cones and evidence limits
findings.text: Ephedra fragilis is dioecious; the female illustration shows fleshy cone structures, not ordinary fruit. The source describes green photosynthetic shoots and arid scrub membership, while noting that cited mycorrhizal evidence concerns other Ephedra species.

findings.label: Wild jujube provides shelter and supports soil formation
findings.text: The UAM factsheet describes the thorny deciduous shrub as shelter for animals and plants, with soil-formation and erosion-control functions. These are source descriptions, not quantified survival benefits for a proposed planting mixture.

findings.label: Oleander toxicity is part of its plant profile
findings.text: The university botanical entry explicitly describes oleander as toxic if ingested. Its presence in watercourse vegetation is not a recommendation for unrestricted planting or use.
